subject: Upper and lower constraints on transformed variables: Logistic vs Jacobian

messages.author: cd58511bd9115a1c
messages.subject: Upper and lower constraints on transformed variables: Logistic vs Jacobian
parts:
What is the best way to constrain multiple, independent,  random walk variables of different scales? e.g.:
parameters{
real<lower=0, upper=1> foo[N];
real<lower=0>          sig_foo;

real<lower=-1000, upper=0> bar[N];
real<lower=0>          sig_foo;
}

model{
...
foo[2:N]=foo[1:(N-1)] + sig_foo;
bar[2:N]=bar[1:(N-1)] + sig_bar;
...
}

given that it is better to reparameterize them to be on the same scale:

parameters{
vector[N]              foo_raw;
real<lower=0>          sig_foo;

vector[N]              bar_raw;
real<lower=0>          sig_foo;
}

transformed parameters{
vector[N]  foo;
vector[N]  bar;

foo[2:N]=foo[1:(N-1)] + sig_foo*foo_raw[1:N];
bar[2:N]=bar[1:(N-1)] + sig_bar*bar_raw[1:N];

...
}

model{
...
foo_raw[1:N] ~ normal(0,1);
bar_raw[1:N] ~ normal(0,1);
...
}
the manual seems to suggest Jacobian adjustments, but I can't find any good example in the manual or message board of implementing both upper and lower bounds for multiple independent variables. How would one go about doing this? Chapter 58 talks about the reverse situation.

An alternative approach that I have tried is to model the final transformed variable as a logistic:
functions
{
     real logistic(real val, real lower_bound, real upper_bound)
     {
          return (upper_bound-lower_bound)*exp(val)/(1+exp(val))+lower_bound;
     }
}

parameters{
vector[N]              foo_raw;
real<lower=0>          sig_foo;

vector[N]              bar_raw;
real<lower=0>          sig_foo;
}

transformed parameters{
//Random walk variables
vector[N]  foo_RW;
vector[N]  bar_RW;

//Constrained via logistic
vector[N]  foo;
vector[N]  bar;


foo_RW[1]= sig_foo*foo_raw[1:N];
bar_RW[1]= sig_bar*bar_raw[1:N];

foo_RW[2:N]=foo_RW[1:(N-1)] + sig_foo*foo_raw[1:N];
bar_RW[2:N]=bar_RW[1:(N-1)] + sig_bar*bar_raw[1:N];

for (n in 1:N){
    foo[n]=logistic(foo_RW[n],0,1);
    bar[n]=logistic(bar_RW[n],-1000,0);
}

...
}

model{
...
     foo_raw[1:N] ~ normal(0,1);
     bar_raw[1:N] ~ normal(0,1);
...
}

Is there any benefit or determent to taking this approach? I have applied the logistic approach to my model (see attached), and while does work, the fit is slow and there needs to be strong control of the sigmas and _RW parameters to keep the random walks within reasonable values, which seems almost to defeat the purpose.

Any thoughts?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Upper and lower constraints on transformed variables: Logistic vs Jacobian
parts:
You found the right chapter. If you look at the upper and lower
bound constraint section (58.4) it shows you how to calculate the Jacobians
for the inverse transforms from an unconstrained representation to one bounded
above and below. We've been meaning to write functions for these in the language
itself but haven't gotten around to it.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Upper and lower constraints on transformed variables: Logistic vs Jacobian
parts:
Then you don't need the Jacobian. The manual's a bit confusing
there in that variables aren't literally sampled---it's a matter
of whether they show up on the left or right of the conditional |,
which is indicated by being on the left of the ~ in a sampling
statement (which is just shorthand to increment the log density).

- Bob
